source.title: GrowCLIP: Data-aware Automatic Model Growing for Large-scale Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
source.authors: Xi Deng; Han Shi; Runhu Huang; Changlin Li; Hang Xu; Jian-Hua Han; J. Kwok; Shen Zhao; Wei Zhang; Xiao-Dan Liang

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies growing vision-language models and reports zero-shot task accuracy, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or determine compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The results in Table 1 compare two vision-language model sizes across CC12M data fractions. They do not test a power-law relationship or prediction. No result measures held-out pretraining loss or the versions' specified behaviour; the reported task accuracies are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: GrowCLIP is a model-growing/NAS method for CLIP under growing data. It cites Kaplan et al. only to motivate that capacity should match data size. It fits no power laws, reports no held-out pretraining loss curves, and makes no extrapolation or compute-optimal analysis. Table 1 is a two-size × four-data-fraction downstream accuracy motivation check, too sparse to bear on any version's power-law form. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses': scaling laws appear only as a citation for the model-size/data-size link.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors propose GrowCLIP (growth architecture selection plus parameter inheriting with momentum) for online CLIP pretraining on growing data. It gains up to 2.3% average zero-shot top-1 over baselines and 1.2% Flickr30K image-to-text R@1. They argue fixed model capacity limits performance as data grows, and offer architecture-design heuristics from growth-dimension ablations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies automatic growth of vision-language contrastive models and downstream task accuracy, not language-model held-out loss scaling or power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that relative performance ranking between the two model sizes depends on the CC12M data fraction.

fits_no_version.finding: On CC12M fractions, CLIP-0.5-ViT-B/16 matches ViT-B/16 at 10% data (6.6 vs 6.5 ImageNet zero-shot). ViT-B/16 leads at 20%, 50% and 100% (11.6/20.9/28.3 vs 11.1/19.0/25.7), with the gap widening as data grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CLIP pretraining, the benefit of a larger model over a smaller one grows with training-data size.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: Only CC12M is used, as the authors note. The results are downstream task accuracies rather than held-out pretraining losses, and the paper does not fit or evaluate power-law predictions.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss vs parameters/tokens/compute, no power-law fit
Table 9 reports growth-dimension accuracy gains, not loss at fixed parameter count
No power-law form fitted for vision-language contrastive pretraining
No fit of downstream accuracy to scale or loss

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The fits_no_version description in the record misstates the 50% cell (the larger model wins there). The rows duplicate each table cell twice.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Loss differences across architectures at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

rows.size_stated: Depth and width are both one half of ViT-B/16.
rows.operation_detail: Compared model sizes after training on different fractions of CC12M.
rows.note: This downstream accuracy comparison does not measure the power-law loss or prediction specified by the claim.
rows.check: This is a motivating check, not a scaling test. The fits_no_version wording is also off: at 10% the models are essentially tied (6.6 vs 6.5), and at 50% the larger model is higher (20.9 vs 19.0), not the smaller one. The authors describe ViT-B/16 as better when data is sufficient.
